1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: Both solutions load the Allen Visual Behavior 2P release through the AllenSDK BehaviorOphysExperiment object and take neural/behaviour/stimulus streams from the same attributes (.ophys_timestamps, .dff_traces, .trials, .running_speed, .eye_tracking). The only difference is the access route: the reference goes through VisualBehaviorOphysProjectCache.from_s3_cache()/get_behavior_ophys_experiment(), the AI opens the local NWB files with BehaviorOphysExperiment.from_nwb_path() and discovers sessions from the released project_metadata/ophys_experiment_table.csv (the same table get_ophys_experiment_table() serves). The AI documented why (the local cache lacks the manifests directory, and get_behavior_ophys_experiment() itself terminates in from_nwb, so the object is identical) and cross-checked that all 284 locally present NWB files and the 29,097 cells in ophys_cells_table.csv were accounted for. This is the same loading decision by a different, equally valid mechanism; the AI additionally parallelises over sessions, which the reference does not.
1-a.code_correctness_justification: select_experiments() enumerates every .nwb file actually present on disk and intersects it with the experiment table, so nothing locally available is silently missed; process_experiment() opens each file once and pulls exactly the documented attributes. The ProcessPoolExecutor.map preserves input order and every job's result (including skips) is collected and reported. Counts in conversion_full_out.txt (168 selected, 165 kept, 37 mice, 28,821 neurons, 42,410 trials) are consistent with the stated selection.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: Identical decision: subjects are mice keyed on mouse_id (the AI reads it from each NWB's metadata, the reference from the experiment table's mouse_id column; they are the same field). Both build a sorted unique subject list and a per-session subject_idx into it. The AI obtains 37 mice, matching the number of distinct mouse_ids in the metadata table for the locally present VisualBehavior experiments.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: str(md['mouse_id']) is carried through per session in res['subject']; subjects = sorted(set(...)) over kept sessions only, and subject_idx is built from the same kept list in the same order as data['neural'], so session-to-subject correspondence cannot drift. verification_full_out.txt lists 37 subjects with 2-9 sessions each, summing to 165.

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: The core split matches: one session per ophys session, restricted to project_code == 'VisualBehavior'. The AI verified (rather than assumed) that this project has exactly one imaging plane per ophys session, so its experiment-level split is equivalent to the reference's grouping by ophys_session_id, and it justified excluding the Multiscope project because its 10.73 Hz frame rate would violate the format requirement that time bins be the same size for all sessions. Beyond the reference, the AI excludes the 71 passive experiments and the 3 sessions with an empty eye_tracking table. Both exclusions are better justified than including them: the AI showed empirically that hit == false_alarm == 0 in every passive session (the lick spout is retracted), so the required 'trial outcome' output is structurally degenerate there and would let a decoder exploit session type, and the reference paper states passive viewing 'was not analyzed here'; sessions with no eye tracking cannot supply the required pupil output at all (the reference's handling would silently label every one of their timepoints as pupil bin 0). The cost is ~30% fewer sessions than the reference retains, which is a real trade-off worth a human's attention, but the rationale is documented, data-driven and paper-supported.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: The passive filter is applied in select_experiments() via ~et.passive.astype(bool) before any file is opened, and the eye-tracking check is applied after opening and returns a logged skip record rather than failing silently. All three skipped sessions and their reason appear in conversion_full_out.txt and in metadata['skipped_sessions'], and 239 local VisualBehavior experiments -> 168 active -> 165 converted is arithmetically consistent with the notes.

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same decision as the reference: trials come from the SDK trials table, the window is the experiment's own [start_time, stop_time) (variable length, spanning pre-change flashes and the post-change response window), and boundaries are found with np.searchsorted on ophys_timestamps. The AI selects rows with go | catch where the reference uses ~aborted & ~auto_rewarded & change_time.notna(); the AI verified these are the same set (hit+miss+FA+CR == n(go union catch) in every session, and it separately audited that no go/catch trial has a NaN change_time). Mean trial length 8.47 s / 262 frames and mean change latency 4.227 s match the whitepaper's ~4.2 s.
1-d.code_correctness_justification: keep = go | catch is applied before anything else is computed, and the per-trial index ranges come from vectorised searchsorted(ts, starts/stops, side='left'), giving a half-open window so consecutive trials cannot share a frame (explicitly audited). The same a:b range slices neural and all five outputs, so no trial can have mismatched lengths; verify_data_format reports no errors or warnings on the full dataset.

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: The substantive filter is the same (go/catch only; sessions need at least 2 trials for the decoder). The AI adds two guards the reference lacks - drop a trial with fewer than 2 ophys frames (0 occurred) and drop a trial containing no non-blink pupil sample (60 of 42,470 trials, 0.14%) - both of which are well justified given pupil diameter is a mandatory output, and both are counted and reported rather than silent. Neither solution filters on engagement, reward rate or lick behaviour, and neither is required to by the instructions. The scale of the extra filtering is negligible, so this is effectively the reference decision plus documented, minor additions.
1-e.code_correctness_justification: The drop rules are implemented exactly as described, with counters (n_drop_short, n_drop_pupil) surfaced in metadata['session_info'] and in the conversion log ('trials dropped: 60 (no pupil sample), 0 (too short)'). The pupil-validity test uses searchsorted over the non-blink sample times restricted to the same [start,stop) window, which correctly tests for at least one real measurement inside the trial. The <2-trial session guard returns a skip record before any output is emitted.

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Both derive neural from dff_traces.dff (the released neuropil-subtracted, demixed, baseline-normalised, detrended dF/F). Notably the AI did not simply default to this: it implemented events and filtered_events (the signal the reference paper actually analyses) and benchmarked all three end-to-end, finding events are non-zero on only ~0.25% of 32 ms frames and decode far worse at per-timepoint resolution (image identity 0.29 vs 0.47 at 20 sessions). It then documented the dF/F choice as a deliberate, measured deviation from the paper. This arrives at the same variable as the human reference with considerably more evidence.
2-a.code_correctness_justification: The default --neural-signal is 'dff' and the full conversion log confirms it was used; the trace matrix is built from ds.dff_traces['dff'] indexed by cell_specimen_id. An independent h5py re-read of processing/ophys/dff/traces/data for 15 random (session, trial, neuron, timepoint) samples matched with np.allclose(atol=1e-6), confirming the stored values really are the released dF/F.

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Both apply no processing beyond assembling the trace matrix and slicing it by trial - no smoothing, normalisation, baseline correction or re-binning; the stored values are the released dF/F cast to float32. The AI tested z-scoring as an alternative, found it changed accuracy by <=0.02 in both directions, and kept the raw released traces, explicitly so that 'the converted neural values *are* the released dF/F'. The reference stacks dF/F across planes; the AI does not need to because the VisualBehavior project has one plane per session (verified).
2-b.code_correctness_justification: The z-score branch is gated on job['zscore'], which is False by default and was not used in the full run. Neuron ordering follows cell_specimen_table index consistently for both the traces and the brain_region_idx labels, so rows cannot be permuted relative to their region labels.

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Both apply no QC beyond what the Allen pipeline has already done. The AI keeps cell_specimen_table.valid_roi == True and reports that this removes nothing (29,097/29,097), which is the same population the reference gets from dff_traces; it also audited for duplicate/NaN cell_specimen_ids and NaN/Inf dF/F (none). Writing the valid_roi filter explicitly is harmless and makes the assumption checkable.
2-c.code_correctness_justification: valid_roi is read from cell_specimen_table and used to index cell_ids, and the same cell_ids drive both the trace matrix and n_neurons; a zero-ROI session would be skipped. Total 28,821 neurons over 165 sessions is consistent with 29,097 over 168 minus the three skipped sessions.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same alignment decision as the reference: the ophys frame clock is the master time base (as the instructions require), trials are aligned to trials.start_time, and the kept frames are those with start_time <= t < stop_time located by np.searchsorted. Metadata records temporal_alignment_event as the trial start, off_start = 0.0 and off_end = None for the variable-length window, matching the reference's 'trial_start' alignment. The AI went further in validating alignment (diagnostic figures overlaying the raw 60 Hz running and 30 Hz pupil streams and the stimulus flash spans on the resampled traces, with the independent trials-table change_time drawn on top).
2-d.code_correctness_justification: One index range a:b per trial slices the neural matrix and all five output rows, so cross-stream alignment is exact by construction rather than by coincidence. searchsorted with side='left' on both boundaries implements the stated half-open window, and i1 can never exceed len(ts), so the slices are always in range.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: Same decision: keep the native ophys frame grid with no rebinning or resampling of the neural data, and compute time_bin_size from the median inter-frame interval. The AI's value, 32.32 ms (30.94 Hz), is the correct single-plane Scientifica rate for the VisualBehavior project (the reference's own notes quote ~11 Hz, which is the Mesoscope rate and does not correspond to the project its code selects). The AI additionally enforces the format requirement that bins be identical across sessions by asserting min/max frame period agree to 1e-4 s and by reporting the observed range - a check the reference omits, and the reason it excluded the 10.73 Hz Multiscope files.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: frame_period_s is the per-session median np.diff(ts); metadata['time_bin_size'] is the median across sessions in ms, with the [32.3100, 32.3300] ms range also stored, and the uniformity assertion passed on the full run. No interpolation or binning is applied to the neural traces anywhere in the script.

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Image identity* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Different source, equally (arguably better) justified. The reference builds image identity from the trials table (initial_image_name before change_time, change_image_name after), so the label is held constant across the 500 ms grey inter-stimulus intervals and across omitted flashes. The AI instead reads the stimulus_presentations table (start_time, end_time, image_name, restricted to the change_detection block) and labels each ophys frame with the image that is physically on screen at that instant, with 'grey' as its own class for the ISI and omitted flashes. The AI's version is a more faithful description of the visual stimulus and is a defensible reading of the instruction's parenthetical ('of the image presented during the non-grey screen'); the reference's is a defensible reading too, since holding the image avoids a dominant 67% grey class. Both are time-varying and both are traceable to reference material (the tutorials' plot_stimuli shades exactly these flash spans). Not a match, but not worse: the resulting decoder reaches 0.405 balanced accuracy on a 17-way problem (6.9x chance).
3-a.code_correctness_justification: The implementation does exactly what the decision states: searchsorted(start, ts, 'right')-1 finds the last flash that has begun, on_screen requires ts < end_time (with NaN end_time from omitted flashes coerced to -inf, so omitted -> grey), and frames before the first flash get valid == False -> grey. An independent h5py rebuild of the whole-session trace from intervals/*_presentations was 100% identical, the recovered flash duration (258.6 ms = 8 frames) matches the 250 ms nominal, and the on-screen fraction 0.331 matches the 250/750 duty cycle.

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Image identity*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: Both map image names to integer codes through a single globally consistent code book covering all 16 images of sets A and B (rather than the per-session 0-7 image_index), and both record the mapping for interpretation. The only difference is that the AI hard-codes the sorted 16-name list (verified against the data) with grey = 0 prepended, so codes are stable no matter which subset of sessions is converted, while the reference derives the sorted list from the sessions actually loaded. The AI also honestly documents the downstream consequence of a globally shared label space - the decoder can predict an image-set-B class on an image-set-A session, producing a benign sklearn warning.
3-b.code_correctness_justification: IMAGE_CODE maps the 16 names to 1..16 and IMAGE_CODE.get(n, 0) sends anything else (including 'omitted') to grey; the edge-case audit confirmed no image name outside the known 16 occurs. output_values[0] is ['grey'] + the 16 names in the same order as the codes, so the label names line up with the integers, and the observed per-image fractions (~0.020 each) are uniform as expected.

3-c.question: How is `output` *Image identity* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same alignment principle as the reference: the image trace lives on the ophys frame grid and is indexed with the identical per-trial frame indices as the neural matrix, so there is no independent alignment step that could drift. The AI's switch points are the flash onset/offset times rather than the trials-table change_time, but both resolve to the same ophys frames (the diagnostic figure shows the identity code changing on exactly the frame where the independent change_time line falls).
3-c.code_correctness_justification: image_all is computed once per session against ts and then sliced as image_all[a:b], the same a:b used for neural. The 100%-identical independent rebuild in the sanity checks covers the alignment as well as the values.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Image change* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: Semantically the same variable from an equivalent source. The reference uses trials.change_time gated on trials.go; the AI uses stimulus_presentations.is_change, which the SDK sets True only on genuine change flashes and False on catch/sham changes. Both therefore give 1 only for real image changes and 0 throughout catch trials. The AI verified the equivalence directly ('one change per GO trial / none per CATCH trial' passed in every session), and using the stimulus table keeps image_change consistent with how it defines image_identity.
4-a.code_correctness_justification: is_change is carried through the same sorted flash arrays used for image identity and combined with the on_screen mask, so the pulse can only occur inside a real flash. The independent h5py rebuild from is_change was 100% identical, and the converted positive fraction (0.0257) matches the analytic expectation P(go) x 0.2511 s / mean trial length = 0.0259.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Image change*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: Neither solution does any processing beyond forming the binary per-frame indicator and storing it with value names ['no_change','change'] - the same decision. The AI additionally validates the resulting base rate against a closed-form expectation.
4-b.code_correctness_justification: change_all is a plain int16 indicator sliced as change_all[a:b] into row 1 of the (5, T) output, and output_values[1] is ['no_change','change'], matching the 0/1 encoding.

4-c.question: How is `output` *Image change* thresholded into categories?
4-c.decision_correctness_justification: Both are binary; they differ in the width of the positive window. The reference marks 750 ms from change_time (one flash plus the following grey interval, the unit the paper assigns events to); the AI marks only the 250 ms during which the changed image is actually on screen. The AI implemented both (--change-window flash|interval), benchmarked them on 20 sessions, and chose the 250 ms window on evidence (image_change 0.640 vs 0.624) and for consistency with its grey-aware definition of image identity. Both satisfy the instruction ('value of 1 right after a change in image identity'), and the AI's choice is if anything the harder, more conservative label - it honestly notes in Step 12 that the GCaMP6f response peaks 200-400 ms after the flash, i.e. partly outside its own positive window. Equally justified, and the alternative was tested rather than assumed.
4-c.code_correctness_justification: The default branch (change_window == 'flash') uses on_screen & is_change, which is exactly the 250 ms flash; the 'interval' branch uses valid & is_change, which extends to the next flash onset (750 ms). The full run used the default, and the notes' claim of ~8 positive frames per go trial is consistent with 250 ms / 32.3 ms.

4-d.question: How is `output` *Image change* aligned with the neural data?
4-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the reference in principle: the indicator is on the ophys frame grid and is sliced with the same per-trial indices as the neural data, so alignment is exact by construction. The AI verified the pulse coincides with the independently obtained trials-table change_time in its diagnostic plots.
4-d.code_correctness_justification: change_all[a:b] uses the identical a:b as neural[:, a:b]; the per-session rebuild from raw is_change matched 100%, and the one-change-per-go-trial/zero-per-catch-trial check passed in all 165 sessions.

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Running speed* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: Identical: ds.running_speed's 'speed' (cm/s) and 'timestamps', with no additional preprocessing on top of the SDK's own unwrapping/transient-correction/low-pass. This is the same stream the reference tutorials' plot_running uses.
5-a.code_correctness_justification: resample_running reads exactly those two columns, drops non-finite samples, and sorts by timestamp before interpolating. The independent h5py rebuild from processing/running/speed/{timestamps,data} reproduced the converted bin trace 100.0000% identically.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Running speed*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same two steps as the reference: linear interpolation onto the ophys time base, then percentile discretisation, with no smoothing or clipping. np.interp vs scipy interp1d is immaterial; the only behavioural difference is at the edges (np.interp constant-extends, interp1d yields NaN), and the AI audited that no trial window falls outside the running-speed coverage (worst margin 300 s / 601 s), so no extrapolation actually occurs.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: The interpolation is done once per session against the full ophys_timestamps vector and then sliced per trial, so all trials share one consistent resampling. The diagnostic figure shows the resampled trace superimposed on the raw 60 Hz signal, and the h5py rebuild matched exactly.

5-c.question: How is `output` *Running speed* thresholded into categories?
5-c.decision_correctness_justification: Different scope, comparably justified. The instruction asks for 'five equal percentile bins' without specifying whether percentiles are global or per session. The reference pools all trial timepoints across all sessions and computes one global set of edges; the AI computes edges per session, over exactly the timepoints that enter the dataset. The AI's rationale is explicit and sound - per-session bins guarantee the equal-percentile property holds within every session and give an exactly balanced 20/20/20/20/20 target, avoiding a situation where session-level differences in behaviour dominate the label - and the edges are stored per session so the mapping back to cm/s is recoverable. The trade-off, which a reviewer should be aware of, is that the same label index means different physical speeds in different sessions, which is a slight mismatch with the decoder's shared readout head. Both choices are defensible; neither is wrong.
5-c.code_correctness_justification: quantile_bins computes the 20/40/60/80th percentiles of the supplied values and assigns bins with searchsorted(..., 'right'), giving indices 0-4; it is called on run_all[frame_idx] where frame_idx is exactly the concatenation of kept trial windows, matching the stated decision. The conversion log shows 0.2000 in every bin, and the edges are saved in metadata['session_info'][i]['running_quintile_edges'].

5-d.question: How is `output` *Running speed* aligned with the neural data?
5-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference: running speed is interpolated onto the ophys timestamps before trial segmentation, so it is indexed by the same frame indices as the neural data and alignment is guaranteed. Both rely on the fact that all streams are recorded on one hardware clock; the AI cites the whitepaper's 100 kHz IO board for this and verified stream coverage of every trial window.
5-d.code_correctness_justification: run_bin_all[a:b] uses the same a:b as neural[:, a:b]. The whole-session bin trace reproduced 100% from raw h5py, which validates the resampling and the indexing together.

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Pupil diameter* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: Different column of the same table, equally justified. The reference uses eye_tracking.pupil_width with rows masked by likely_blink; the AI uses eye_tracking.pupil_area, drops non-finite/non-positive values, and converts to an effective diameter 2*sqrt(area/pi). The AI's claim that pupil_area is NaN exactly where likely_blink is True is verifiable and I confirmed it directly on a release NWB file (12,500 blink flags, 12,500 NaN areas, exact agreement), so its blink handling is equivalent to the reference's. Area is at least as good a pupil-size estimate as a single ellipse axis, and the whitepaper reports pupil area; the monotone area->diameter transform leaves the quintiles unchanged. Neither choice is better-grounded than the other.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: resample_pupil filters on np.isfinite(a) & (a > 0), sorts by timestamp, converts area to diameter, and interpolates - exactly the stated decision - and also returns the valid sample times used for the per-trial pupil-validity test. The independent h5py rebuild from acquisition/EyeTracking/pupil_tracking/area plus likely_blink reproduced the converted bins 100.0000% identically, which confirms the NaN/likely_blink equivalence holds in practice.

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Pupil diameter*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same pipeline as the reference: remove blink samples, linearly interpolate the surviving samples onto the ophys time base (which also bridges the blink gaps), then discretise into five percentile bins. The AI adds the area->diameter conversion (monotone, no effect on bins) and records the per-session blink fraction.
6-b.code_correctness_justification: The blink mask is applied before interpolation, so blink values cannot leak into neighbouring frames, and the plot panel shows the interpolated line passing through every raw non-blink sample. The independent rebuild matched 100% with np.allclose bin edges.

6-c.question: How is `output` *Pupil diameter* thresholded into categories?
6-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same difference as for running speed: per-session rather than global quintiles. Here the AI's argument is the stronger of the two, since pupil size is measured in camera pixels and depends on camera zoom, eye position and rig, so a globally pooled percentile split partly encodes session identity rather than arousal. The reference's global binning is still a legitimate literal reading of 'five equal percentile bins'. Equally justified; the per-session edges are stored so nothing is lost.
6-c.code_correctness_justification: quantile_bins is applied to pupil_all[frame_idx] per session exactly as for running speed, yielding 0.200 of timepoints in each of the five bins, with pupil_quintile_edges saved per session.

6-d.question: How is `output` *Pupil diameter* aligned with the neural data?
6-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference: interpolated onto the ophys timestamps before segmentation and sliced with the same per-trial indices. The AI adds a guarantee the reference does not have - a trial is dropped unless it contains at least one real (non-blink) pupil sample - so no trial's pupil label is produced purely by interpolation across a long gap, and it audited that no trial window falls outside the eye-tracking coverage.
6-d.code_correctness_justification: pup_bin_all[a:b] uses the same a:b as neural, and the j0/j1 searchsorted pair correctly counts non-blink samples inside [start_time, stop_time) for the validity test. 60 trials were dropped by this rule and are reported.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Trial outcome* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: Identical: the four mutually exclusive boolean trials-table columns hit, miss, false_alarm, correct_reject, in the same order, giving codes 0-3. The AI strengthens this with an assertion that every kept go/catch trial has exactly one True (the reference silently falls back to an 'other'/-1 code), and verified against a direct scan of the raw tables (hit .3196 / miss .5550 / FA .0191 / CR .1062).
7-a.code_correctness_justification: The four columns are stacked and np.argmax gives the code; the assertion would abort the session if the one-hot assumption failed, and it did not fire on any of the 165 sessions. output_values[4] lists the four names in the same order as the codes.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Trial outcome*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same decision: a single integer code per trial, broadcast across every timepoint of the trial so the static label lives in the same (5, T) array as the time-varying outputs - which the format spec explicitly prefers. The AI also reports the consequence honestly (this output has the largest train/validation gap, 1.49, because the effective sample size is the number of trials while the model sees timepoints) rather than glossing over it.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: out[4] = outcome[k] broadcasts the scalar over the T-length row, and the sanity checks confirmed the value is constant within each trial and matches the raw trials table. Per-timepoint and per-trial outcome fractions are both reported and differ only as expected from trial-length weighting.

8.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
8.decision_correctness_justification: The AI's handling is more careful than the reference's on every axis. Where the reference maps NaN running/pupil to bin 0 - which silently mislabels missing data as the lowest quintile and would apply to entire sessions that have no eye tracking at all - the AI drops sessions with no eye tracking (3) and trials with no valid non-blink pupil sample (60 of 42,470), so no fabricated label enters the dataset, and it counts and reports every drop in metadata rather than losing it silently. Omitted flashes (NaN end_time) and frames preceding the first flash are given the semantically correct 'grey' label instead of being left undefined. It adds assertions on one-hot trial outcomes and on frame-period uniformity, and it ran a systematic edge-case audit over all 165 sessions (NaN change_time, duplicate/NaN cell ids, NaN/Inf dF/F, non-monotonic timestamps, overlapping trials, unknown image names, trial windows outside each stream's coverage), all clean. The reference's broad try/except around a whole session is coarser: it would swallow a genuine bug as a skipped session.
8.code_correctness_justification: Each documented case has a matching guard in the code (eye-tracking skip, isfinite masks before interpolation, np.nan_to_num(end, nan=-inf) for omitted flashes, valid mask for pre-first-flash frames, the two per-trial drop rules, the <2-trial session guard, and the plotting try/except that cannot mask a conversion error because it only wraps make_processing_plot). The counters and skip reasons appear in the full-run log, and the format verifier reports no errors or warnings.

9-a.question: What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same conclusion as the reference - loading each experiment's data dominates and is I/O bound - but the AI established it by measurement rather than assertion: it instruments open/neural/behavior/assemble/total per session and prints them, showing 2.7-6.4 s to open the NWB and materialise the trace matrix versus ~0.05 s for all resampling and ~0.05 s for trial assembly, plus 9.2 s to pickle the 8.38 GB output. It also acted on the finding (16 worker processes), bringing the full conversion to 61 s versus the instructions' 15-minute budget.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: The timers bracket exactly the stages they name and are reported per session in conversion_full_out.txt; the aggregate wall time printed (51.3 s processing + 9.2 s write = 60.7 s total) is consistent with the per-session numbers and the worker count.

9-b.question: What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: The AI vectorised substantially more than the reference did and documented the reasoning. It resamples every stream once per session onto the full ophys timestamp vector so trials become pure array slices (its own note: '~250x fewer interp calls' than per-trial interpolation), finds all trial boundaries with two vectorised searchsorted calls, and parallelises across sessions - whereas the reference iterates trials with iterrows() and does per-trial searchsorted and per-trial list building. The residual loops the AI leaves (the per-neuron col.loc[cid] trace copy, the per-trial drop-rule loop that could be a boolean mask, the frame_idx comprehension) are real but bounded by <=666 cells or <=400 trials and are negligible against the measured 2.7-6.4 s file open; the per-neuron .loc loop is the one worth fixing, since np.vstack(col.values) would avoid up to 666 pandas index lookups per session. Its self-assessment is accurate as far as it goes, though it does not name that particular loop.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: The claimed vectorisations are present as described: np.interp over the whole timestamp vector, vectorised searchsorted for i0/i1/j0/j1, stimulus lookup by searchsorted over flash onsets, and ProcessPoolExecutor over sessions. The measured 0.31 s/session amortised is consistent with those claims.
